2027-04-09.title: Friday of the Second Week of Easter
readings: They rejoiced that they were considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the sake of the name
One thing I seek: to dwell in the house of the Lord (or: Alleluia)
He distributed to those who were seated as much as they wanted
2027-04-09.alt: Easter weekday of the Second Week of Easter. The Alleluia is sung before the Gospel; the Regina Caeli replaces the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white. Friday: keep the Friday penance as your bishops' conference directs.
2027-04-09.verse: Then Jesus took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated; so also the fish, as much as they wanted.
theo: The council is enraged and wants to put the apostles to death. Then one man stands up: Gamaliel, “a Pharisee in the council… a teacher of the law, respected by all the people.” He is the teacher at whose feet Saul of Tarsus was trained, and later Jewish tradition honours him as one of the great masters of the Law. He has the apostles sent out and gives the council a lesson in patience drawn from recent history: Theudas and Judas the Galilean both gathered followers and both came to nothing. “So in the present case, I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone; because if this plan or this undertaking is of human origin, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them.” Gamaliel is not a Christian, but he is a just man who fears God, and his counsel saves the apostles' lives. The Church has been grateful to him ever since; a later Christian legend even counted him among the friends of the first disciples. The apostles are flogged and released, and Luke records the astonishing reaction: “they rejoiced that they were considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the sake of the name. And every day in the temple and at home they did not cease to teach and proclaim Jesus as the Messiah.” The Psalm is their song: “The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?”

From today until the end of the Third Week of Easter the weekday Gospels walk through the sixth chapter of St John, the great chapter of the Bread of Life. It begins with a sign. “The Passover, the festival of the Jews, was near,” John notes, and a large crowd follows Jesus up the mountain by the Sea of Galilee. Jesus tests Philip: “Where are we to buy bread for these people to eat?” Philip calculates: six months' wages would not be enough. Andrew finds “a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are they among so many people?” Barley loaves were the bread of the poor, and they recall the prophet Elisha, who fed a hundred men with twenty barley loaves. Jesus has the people sit on the green grass; then he “took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them.” The Greek word for giving thanks is eucharistein. The evangelist wants us to see the Eucharist in this meal, celebrated near the Passover. After all have eaten “as much as they wanted,” Jesus says: “Gather up the fragments left over, so that nothing may be lost,” and twelve baskets are filled. The Church still treats every fragment of the consecrated Host with that same care. When the crowd tries to seize him and make him king, Jesus withdraws alone to the mountain. He will not be a king who only hands out bread; he will be the King who gives his own flesh as bread.
outline: Ask: what small thing do you have that Jesus could multiply?
Point 1 · If it is of God
Point 2 · Worthy to suffer for the name
Point 3 · Five loaves and twelve baskets
The sign of the Bread, near Passover.
“Gather up the fragments left over, so that nothing may be lost.”
live: Give Jesus one small gift today, an hour, a talent, a sum of money, and let him use it for others.
Do not waste food today; share leftovers with someone who needs them, or give the price of one meal to the poor.
2027-04-09.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you fed the multitude with five barley loaves and gave thanks to the Father for the bread. Give us the wisdom of Gamaliel to recognize the work of God, the joy of the apostles in suffering for your name, and the generosity of the boy who gave you all he had. Feed us with the Bread of Life, and let nothing of your gifts be lost. Who live and reign for ever and ever. Amen.
altar: Jesus took the loaves, gave thanks and distributed them. At every Mass he does the same, and the bread he gives is no longer bread but his Body. Like the disciples gathering the fragments, the Church reverences every particle of the consecrated Host.

quick: Gamaliel told the council: if this work is of God, you cannot overthrow it.
The apostles were flogged and rejoiced to suffer for the name of Jesus.
Jesus fed five thousand people with five barley loaves and two fish, and twelve baskets were left over.
2027-04-09.action: Give the value of one meal today to a poor family or to the parish charity box.
2027-04-09.question: What is my “five loaves,” and have I placed it in Jesus' hands?

family.explain: A huge crowd was hungry. A boy had only five small loaves and two fish. He gave them to Jesus. Jesus thanked God, and shared them, and everyone ate as much as they wanted! There were twelve baskets left over.
family.intention: We pray for children who go to sleep hungry tonight.
family.ask: Ask: “What small thing can I give Jesus today?” Each one names something, and the family helps them do it.

illus: In a hill parish in Idukki the Sunday school children decided during Lent to bring one coin each week for a boy in their class whose father had died. By Easter the tin held barely enough for a pair of school shoes. A shopkeeper in town heard the story, added the rest of the uniform and a year's books, and told the parish priest: I could not let those children's coins be wasted. Five loaves become twelve baskets when someone gives first.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, Bread of Life, we bring you our little loaves; bless them, break them and share them. Alleluia. Amen.
share: If it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them (Acts 5:39). Do I trust that God's work will last even when it looks weak?
They rejoiced that they were considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the sake of the name (Acts 5:41). How do I bear insult for my faith?
There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish (John 6:9). What small gift is the Lord asking from me?
pm.resp: One thing I seek: to dwell in the house of the Lord.
interc: For the Church, that she may feed the hungry with bread and with the Word.
For Christians who suffer insult or violence for the name of Jesus, that they may know Easter joy.
For leaders and judges, that they may have the wisdom and justice of Gamaliel.
For the hungry of our village and our world, and for an end to the waste of food.
For our group, that we may give Jesus what little we have.
pm.close: Father, your Son fed the multitude and gives himself as the Bread of Life. Make us generous and grateful. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, the council wants to kill the apostles, and a wise teacher named Gamaliel stands up. He says: if this plan is of human origin, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them (Acts 5:38–39). Two thousand years later, the Church is still here. Not because we are strong, but because the work is God's.

The apostles are flogged, and they go out rejoicing that they were worthy to suffer for the name of Jesus. What a change from the frightened men behind locked doors! The risen Lord does not take away the suffering, but he fills it with joy.

In the Gospel a boy gives Jesus five barley loaves and two fish. It seems like nothing. Jesus takes them, gives thanks, and distributes them, and five thousand people eat as much as they want (John 6:11). Our gifts always seem small. But in Jesus' hands they become enough, and more than enough.

Notice the words: he took, he gave thanks, he distributed. These are the words of the Mass. And at the end Jesus says: gather up the fragments, so that nothing may be lost. At the altar today he will feed us with the true Bread, his own Body. Let us bring him our five loaves, and leave nothing of his gift wasted. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, a little boy had a small lunch: five small breads and two fish. He gave it all to Jesus. Jesus thanked God and shared it, and more than five thousand people ate! When we give Jesus even a little, he can do great things with it. What will you give Jesus today?

intro: Theme: “He distributed them to those who were seated, as much as they wanted.”
Gamaliel's counsel, the joy of suffering for the name, and the sign of the loaves.

sub: A respected teacher of the Law.
q: The human mind may devise many plans, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will be established.
So in the present case, I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone; because if this plan or this undertaking is of human origin, it will fail;
points.apply: Before judging a new movement or person in the Church, pray for a week and ask: could this be of God?

points.h: Worthy to suffer for the name
sub: Every day, in the Temple and at home.
q: The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The LORD is the stronghold of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?
As they left the council, they rejoiced that they were considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the sake of the name.
points.apply: When you are mocked for your faith this week, answer with a smile and a silent prayer for the one who mocks.

q: So he repeated, “Give it to the people and let them eat, for thus says the LORD, ‘They shall eat and have some left.’”
When they were satisfied, he told his disciples, “Gather up the fragments left over, so that nothing may be lost.”
points.apply: Receive Communion this Sunday with special reverence, and at home waste no food for one whole week.

concl: What is of God cannot be overthrown, and those who suffer for Jesus' name rejoice.
Jesus takes our little gifts, gives thanks and feeds the multitude, and gives himself as the Bread of Life.
2027-04-09.resolve: Offer Jesus one “five loaves” gift each day this week.
